Falling film evaporation on enhanced tubes, part 1:
Experimental results for pool boiling, onset-of-dryout and
falling film evaporation
Marcel Christians, John Richard Thome*
Laboratory of Heat and Mass Transfer (LTCM), Ecole Polytechnique Fe ́de ́rale de Lausanne, ME G1 465, Station 9, CH-1015 Lausanne,

a b s t r a c t
Horizontal falling film evaporators have the potential of displacing flooded evaporators as
the standard in the refrigeration industry due to compelling advantages, such as smaller
refrigerant charge and lower pressure drop. However, there is a need to improve the
understanding of falling film evaporation mechanisms to provide accurate thermal design
methods. In this work, falling film evaporation measurements on a single tube, a vertical
row of ten horizontal tubes and a small tube bundle with three rows of 10 tubes each are
presented. Two enhanced boiling tubes, the Wolverine Turbo-B5 and the Wieland Gewa-B5,
were tested using R-134a and R-236fa. The tests were carried out at a saturation temperature of Tsat 1⁄4 5 C, film Reynolds numbers ranging from 0 to 3000, and heat fluxes between
15 and 90 kW m 2 in pool boiling and falling film configurations. A visualization study was
performed under diabatic conditions to study the flow.

Introduction
In industrial applications, falling film evaporators show
several advantages compared to flooded evaporators, particularly in terms of higher cycle efficiency, reduced costs and
a smaller environmental impact due to its reduced charge of
refrigerant. The pressure drop is small as the liquid flows only
due to gravity and this reduces the temperature lift of the
compressor. This type of heat exchanger has been studied over
the years in terms of effects such as the liquid feed flow rate,

tube surface phenomena, tube spacing and heat flux, among
others. A large majority of the studies have been performed
using water or ammonia, due to the large potential of falling
film evaporators in Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion and
actual use in desalination. Falling film evaporation can also be
segregated into conditions with or without nucleate boiling in
the film. The present study considers only the former.
Recent studies involving pool boiling at conditions similar
to those being investigated in this study are presented in
Table 1. The majority of these studies have been discussed by
Roques and Thome (2007a). There are three main additions to
the studies discussed previously, namely those of Habert
(2009), Agostini (2008) and Gorgy (2008).
Gorgy (2008) tested four different combinations: R-134a on
a smooth tube, R-123 on a smooth tube, R-134a on a Turbo-Bii
HP tube, and R-123 on a Turbo Bii-LP tube. A modified Wilson
plot method was utilized to measure the heat transfer coeffi-
cients. The one meter long test tube's outer diameter was
19.05 mm. Tests were conducted with a single tube test
section, in which the test tube was water-heated. All tests
were conducted at a saturation temperature of 4.44 C. Results
showed that the heat transfer coefficient increased with heat
flux for all cases.
Habert (2009) tested the pool boiling performance of the
Turbo-EDE2, Gewa-C LW, Gewa-B4 and a plain tube using
refrigerants R-134a and R-236fa at saturation temperatures of
5, 10 and 20 C. The tubes tested were 19.05 mm in diameter,
and 0.554 m long. An indirect method was utilized to infer the
pool boiling heat transfer coefficient (modified Wilson Plot
method). Using the plain tube, the study generated results
similar to those expected from the literature; the heat transfer
measurements, the values of the correlations and the trends
are similar to the results of citetstephan1992, Stephan and
Abdelsalam (1980) and Cooper (1984). The Gewa-C LW,
a tube designed for condensation, behaved in a similar
fashion. The two enhanced evaporation tubes, on the other
hand, showed decreasing heat transfer with increasing heat
flux. The trend of these results are similar to those found by
Roques and Thome (2007a).

The enhanced boiling process is different from normal
nucleate boiling in cavities. Evaporation occurs both on the
external surface, and inside its re-entrant channels. Thus,
there are four possible ways for heat to be dissipated (Bergles,
1988; Thome, 1990).
1. As latent heat generating vapor within the re-entrant
channels.
2. As latent heat into bubbles growing on the outside surface
of the enhancement.
3. As sensible heat to the liquid, pumped through the re-
entrant channels and back out.
4. As sensible heat to the liquid in the external thermal
boundary layer.
Structured surfaces promote nucleate boiling in the film at
modest temperature differences, enhance convection within
the film and provide an increase in heat transfer area. The
parameters that influence the enhancement are mainly the
shape, geometry and surface area of the cavities. The nucleation site density also plays an important role. For porous
coatings, the principal parameters are the particle size, the
coating thickness and the porosity. The nucleation site
density has been correlated as proportional to the heat
transfer coefficient. Chien and Webb (1998a, b) investigated
the effect of pore diameter, pore pitch and tunnel shape using
R-11 and R-123. They found that there exists an optimal pore
diameter and pore pitch for a specific heat flux range.
However, the determination of the above parameters is purely
empirical, and difficult to ascertain (Poniewski and Thome,
2008).
In comparison to pool boiling, experimental data for
boiling in thin films are relatively scarce, as shown in the
reviews of Thome (2002) and Ribatski and Jacobi (2005). Chyu
and Bergles (1985) investigated falling film heat transfer
mechanisms and defined three flow regimes. For the case of
saturated falling films, convective heat transfer leads to
evaporation at the liquidevapor interface. With an increase of
heat flux, nucleate boiling occurs; vapor bubbles grow and are
carried along by the film flow such that both thin falling film
evaporation and nucleate boiling play a role in the heat
transfer process, depending mainly on the heat flux and liquid
mass flow. Moeykens and Pate (1994) and Zeng et al. (1996)
among others published mean heat transfer coefficient data
for each tube in their row/bundle tests.
Chien and Webb (1998a, b) tested enhanced surfaces
similar to the Turbo-B using R-11 and R-123. It was observed
that, at low heat flux, the tubes having smaller total open
areas (that is, the sum of the cavity areas) gave higher heat
transfer coefficients. At higher heat fluxes, tubes having larger
total open areas yielded higher heat transfer performance.
They reported a cross-over characteristic between the two
areas. If the total open area was too large at low heat flux, the
re-entrant tunnels became flooded by liquid and the heat
transfer coefficient decreased. If the total open area was too
small at high heat fluxes, the tunnels dried out due to inadequate liquid supply. Chien and Webb (1998c) also performed
a visualization study that supported these trends.
Moeykens et al. (1995) observed that enhanced boiling
surfaces gave higher performance than finned tubes but lower
performance than enhanced condensing surfaces used for
evaporation. They noted an increase of heat transfer coeffi-
cient with heat flux up to a specific heat flux, after which, with
any further increase in heat flux, the heat transfer coefficient
decreased. This was probably due to partial dryout.
Roques and Thome (2007a, b) tested three different
enhanced surfaces: Gewa-B, Turbo-Bii and High-Flux. Similar
trends for each surface were found, as well as a strong
dependence of heat transfer on heat flux. The High-Flux tube
achieved up to three times better performance than the other
tubes tested. A falling film multiplier, Kff, was defined as the
ratio between falling film evaporation and pool boiling heat
transfer coefficients on the same tube at the same heat flux,
and gave values between 1 and 2, depending on the enhanced
surface and the experimental conditions, meaning that the
film had a tendency to enhance the heat transfer performance. In general, at low heat fluxes, falling film achieves
better performance than pool boiling. This might be due to
enhanced convective effects in the falling film. At high heat
fluxes, nucleate boiling was the dominant heat transfer mode
and thus the convective effect tended to disappear and the
performances became comparable to those in pool boiling.
According to the authors, the trend for falling film evaporation
is made up of two distinct regions: a plateau corresponding to
an all-wet nucleate boiling-dominated regime where the heat
transfer coefficient varies little with the flow rate, a point of
onset-of-dryout, and a partially wet regime with nucleate
boiling in the remaining film with a thus rapidly decreasing
heat transfer coefficient tending towards the vapor phase
natural convection coefficient at complete dryout. Hence, the
onset-of-dryout is an important part of the heat transfer
process and its modeling.
Habert and Thome (2010) tested three enhanced surfaces,
the Gewa-B4, Turbo-EDE2 and the Gewa-C LW, a condensation tube. The tests were performed using R-134a and R-
236fa. Tests in single-array mode, similar to those of Roques
(2004), were performed. Using the Gewa-C LW, Kff values of
2.5e3 were found near the onset-of-dryout Reynolds number
using R-134a and R-236fa respectively, at a heat flux of
20 kW m 2. However, most of the data lie close to 1, indicating similar performance under falling film and pool boiling
conditions. The performance of the tube did not vary much
with choice of refrigerant. Both the Gewa-B4 and the Turbo-
EDE2 show similar trends to the previous generation's (that
is, tubes tested by Roques); however, due to the improved
performance, the uncertainty in the measurements also
increased. Heat transfer coefficients close to those measured
by Roques for the High-Flux tube were measured. The falling
film multiplier varied between 1 and 2, with falling film
performing best at lower heat fluxes, as shown in previous
studies.
The objectives of the present study are to (i) characterize
the water-side enhancement factor of different enhanced
tubes using the modified Wilson plot method, (ii) measure
local pool boiling coefficients at 5, 10 and 15 C for heat fluxes
ranging from 20 to 80 kW m 2, (iii) measure local heat transfer
coefficients at 5 C on a one-row horizontal tube array and on
a small three-row bundle for heat fluxes of 20, 40 and

2.
Experimental facility
The experimental setup is comprised of three circuits,
namely, the refrigerant, water-glycol, and water circuits. The
refrigerant
circuit
is
shown
schematically
in
Fig.
1.
It
comprises an electrically heated evaporator (1) to maintain
the desired saturation condition, a condenser (5) to balance
the heat load on the system, and the test section itself (4).
In the refrigerant circuit, starting from the flooded evaporator (1), the refrigerant flows through the filter (not shown)
and the subcooler (6) to the oil-free self-lubricating gear pump
(7). Parallel to the pump, bypass piping is installed so that,
together with a frequency controller on the pump, the desired
liquid flow rate can be accurately set. A Coriolis mass flow
meter (8) follows, after which an electric heater (9) is installed
to bring the liquid close to saturation conditions at the test
section inlet (less than 0.5 K from saturation). At this point, the
liquid enters the test section and is distributed uniformly on
the top row of the heated tubes. Special care has been taken in
the distributor design in order to achieve uniform liquid
distribution on the top tube. Once the liquid leaves the
distributor, it falls onto the top of the heated tube array on
which the liquid in the test section is partially evaporated; the
residual liquid leaves the test section by gravity. From the exit
of the test section, the liquid flows back to the flooded
evaporator by the effect of gravity. The vapor generated in the
test section is sucked out at the bottom of the test section.
After exiting the test section from the bottom, it flows to the
condenser, and the liquid drops by gravity back to the flooded
evaporator. The amount of vapor flow can be controlled by
increasing the heat input in the flooded evaporator, which in
turn
generates
more
vapor.
Consequently,
to
maintain
a constant system pressure, the cooling load on the auxiliary
condenser is increased to balance the thermal heat load. In
these tests, it was attempted to maintain the vapor velocity as
low as possible, such that vapor shear effects were minimized.
The water circuit (not shown) is responsible for the heating
effect in the test section. The water is driven through the test
tubes by a centrifugal pump. An electronic speed-controller,
together with a bypass line, ensures good precision in any
water mass flow adjustment. The water flows through two
liquideliquid heat exchangers; the first is cooled with industrial water sourced from Lake Geneva at a constant temperature of 7 C, while the second is heated with hot water from
a closed-loop circuit heated by a heat pump. This water has its
flow rate set by a computer-controlled valve. The water
temperature at the test section inlet is thus automatically
maintained constant. The total water mass flow rate is
measured with a Coriolis flow meter (not shown). Before
entering the test section, the test-line water flow is split into
five subcircuits, each supplying to two tubes in the test section
connected in series. Each subcircuit has two tube passes; i.e.,
water goes in the first tube in one direction (left to right) and
comes back through the copper tube just above in the opposite
direction. This setup keeps the film flow rate uniform along
the axial length of the tube after each of the sets of two tubes
to avoid maldistribution that occurs in one-pass test setups.
A water-glycol mixture from a network installation is used as
a cold source for the auxiliary condenser.

The test section is a rectangular stainless-steel vessel
with six large windows situated at the front and rear in
order to have full visual access into the experimental setup,
to observe the flow on the tubes. The copper test tubes had
a nominal outer diameter of 19.05 mm and a length of
554 mm. In total, ten instrumented tubes (i.e., five sub-
circuits) were installed at an industry-standard pitch of
22.3 mm and arranged in one of two possible configurations.
For single-array tests, these ten tubes were installed horizontally in a vertical array. For bundle tests, two additional
vertical arrays of ten horizontal tubes were installed on
either side of the central array using equal vertical and
horizontal pitches (See Figure 3.7 of Christians (2010)).
Falling film conditions were created on these two rows using
two
sets
of
two
high-performance
condensing
tubes
installed on both sides of the distributor, through which cold
glycol is run. These four tubes provided the condensate
overfeed for the side rows. The glycol mass flow rate was
controlled to regulate the amount of condensate being
generated.
To
further
fine
tune
the
amount
of
heat
exchanged, a three-way valve is installed. The glycol flow
rate through each side could be manually controlled such
that there was no imbalance in the heat extraction between
the two sides.
Hot water was pumped through the side-array tubes;
however, unlike the center column, the water went through
all the side tubes in ten passes (rather than the two passes in
the center column for each pair of tubes). The water flow rate
through each side-array could be controlled in a similar
fashion to the glycol overfeed circuit, such that the waterheated side-array heat transfer remain balanced.
A stainless-steel tube with an external diameter of 8 mm
was inserted inside each of the copper test tubes (in bundle
conditions, only in the ten tubes in the central horizontal
column). Pairs of thermocouples were located at three positions axially along the stainless steel tube, protruding out
through holes to measure the temperature of the water in the
annulus between the stainless steel tube and the copper
tubes. At every location, one thermocouple is facing upward
and one is facing downward. A copper wire with a rectangular
cross section wound helically around the stainless steel tube
promoted mixing, and further increased the water-side heat
transfer coefficient.
Pressure transducers connected to the test section above
and below the array of tubes were used to measure the vapor
pressure in the test section. The vapor temperature in the test
section was measured above and below the tube array using
sheathed thermocouples. The temperatures of the liquid
entering and leaving the test section, as well as the vapor
leaving the test section, were measured.

For experiments involving overfeed, the film flow rate of
the liquid arriving on the first tube was evaluated from the
measured mass flow rate and the tube length, assuming that
the refrigerant is at saturation conditions. The mass flow of
refrigerant evaporating on the first tube is calculated by an
energy balance on differential elements and subtracted from
the film flow rate arriving on the first tube to obtain the film
flow rate at the top of the second tube and so on. This means
an ideal one-dimensional downward flow is assumed on the
tube rows and assumes that all the liquid flows from one tube
to the next without leaving the tube row. The two-pass water
design gives a nearly uniform axial film distribution along the
tube array after each pair of tubes. The saturation temperature, as well as the transport and thermodynamic properties,
are calculated according to REFPROP (National Institute of
Standards and Technology, 2002) from the mean of the pressures measured by pressure transducers above and below the
tube array.
Tests were conducted by gradually decreasing the liquid
film flow rate on the top tube at a fixed heat flux. The data
were logged only if steady state conditions were attained.

the refrigerants are essentially the same. Experimentally, it
was not possible to reach the lowest heat fluxes using the

for this tube are lower than the corresponding Wolverine

made as no publications with the present new enhanced tube

noted that these tubes were developed for applications using

Experimental results for falling film in
single array and in bundle configurations
The experimental conditions are shown in Table 2. For the
single-array tests, a single vertical row of horizontal tubes was
tested. In bundle conditions, only the center array of ten tubes
was instrumented. Furthermore, as in Christians et al. (2010b),
the side-array condensate overfeed and side-array heat
transfer rates could be modified, thus testing was performed
to investigate the effect of the side-array conditions might
have had on the measured heat transfer coefficients. As
shown in Christians (2010), the different conditions tested did
not have any noticeable effect on the measured heat transfer
results. Furthermore, it was found that the single-array and
the bundle results were the same. Thus, the data from the
single-array and bundle tests are presented together for tubes
Turbo-B5 and Gewa-B5 in Figs. 6 and 7, respectively.

heat flux. Due to the high experimental uncertainties, only
data with uncertainties smaller than 45% are shown. This

grows exponentially as the heat flux is decreased not only
because the temperature gradient in the water is smaller
(than at higher heat fluxes), but also due to the fact that the
temperature difference between the refrigerant and the water
decreases as well. At the moment, for these enhanced tubes
and heat fluxes of less than 20 kW m 2, the experimental
superheat is on the order of 0.5 C. Keeping in mind that the
uncertainty of the thermocouples used to measure the

usability. The Gewa-B5 required a smaller superheat (than the

Compared to the pool boiling results of Figs. 4 and 5,
completely different trends are achieved. First, the progressive heat transfer decrease with increasing heat flux found in
all pool boiling experimental data (even the Turbo-B5/R-134a
combination had a slight negative trend) is not found in the
falling film evaporation data. As described by Roques and
Thome (2007a), a heat transfer plateau is reached when the
overfeed is large enough such that partial dryout does not
occur. At Reynolds numbers lower than this threshold, there
is a quasi-monotonic decrease in heat transfer performance.
In these results, there does not seem to be a very strong heat
flux dependence, as the scatter in the plateau for all heat
fluxes tested is large. This results in trends that are difficult to
study. From the comparison of the two data sets, it can be seen
that the falling film conditions enhanced the heat transfer
process, especially in the case of the Turbo-B5. This is shown
in Figs. 8 and 9. In these figures, it can be seen that the heat
flux has a larger influence on the falling film multiplier, with
higher values of Kff for higher heat fluxes. This is of course due

film process is not only advantageous from a charge reduction
point of view. The decrease in performance typically seen
when designing for low pressure refrigerants can be seen to be
seriously mitigated; in fact, the results show that the use of
falling film allowed the heat transfer performance in R-236fa
to be very close, if not the same, to the performance of R-134a
of these tubes. An added advantage of using falling film in low
pressure refrigerants is that the submergence effects are also
decreased (due to not having a large liquid level in the
evaporator).
As the reader may recall, the refrigerant film Reynolds
numbers are calculated assuming one-dimensional flow from
one tube to the next. However, during experimentation, some
tubes showed splash-out and slinging. This loss of refrigerant
to the side-arrays (when in bundle mode) is not quantifiable,
and thus errors are introduced into the presented Reynolds
numbers when some liquid leaves the film. This is the main
culprit for some of the scatter evidenced in the data which
happen to have lower heat transfer performance than expected at specific Reynolds numbers. This is evident in the

Since the Reynolds numbers presented are calculated and are
dependent on the basic assumption that there is no splashout, when this assumption is no longer valid an error is
introduced into the calculated Reynolds numbers such that

Onset-of-dryout
The onset-of-dryout was first experimentally characterized at
the LTCM laboratory by Roques (2004), in a separate set of
experiments in which the film flow rate was decreased in
small steps from a high value at a fixed heat flux. The transition from fully wet to dryout was found to occur at a film
flow rate just at the first dryout patch formation. A simple
linear correlation was made. Later, the criterion based on Kff
defined by Ribatski and Thome (2007) was used to more
objectively study the film breakdown (Ribatski and Thome,
2007; Habert, 2009), as the method first utilized by Roques
(2004) was dependent on a subjective visual analysis of the
flow over a tube. The criterion is defined as

7.
Conclusion
Experimental data collected for tubes Turbo-B5 and Gewa-B5
using refrigerants R-134a and R-236fa in both pool boiling and
falling film tests were presented and discussed. The trends in
the pool boiling results were compared to those found in
previous studies for earlier-generations of these tubes. In pool
boiling, the tubes performed better than the tubes tested by
Roques (2004) and Habert (2009), and showed less dependence
on the applied heat flux. The falling film heat transfer data were
presented for both tubes and refrigerants utilized. No additional bundle effects could be found when testing in bundle
configuration compared to single array tests. A falling film
multiplier, relating the increase in heat transfer performance
when using falling films versus pool boiling was calculated for
the falling film measurements and presented. In terms of
refrigerants, it was seen that R-134a outperformed R-236fa, as
was expected, since these tubes are designed for use with R-
134a. However, the degradation was smaller when testing in
falling film than in pool boiling. The onset-of-dryout threshold
Reynolds numbers were presented for the two tubes and
refrigerants tested. These experimental data show that low
heat flux measurements using thermocouples are nearing the
limits of their applicability, since the majority of the data are
too uncertain to be used. This forces studies of next-generation
tubes toboth start usinghigh accuracy RTDs (achallenge for the
instrumentation used at the LTCM) and to start taking advantage of differential RTD temperature measurements, which
retain the uncertainty of a single RTD ( 0.03 K).The data pre-
sented here are utilized in part 2 of Christians and Thome (2010)
to generate new prediction methods.
